data.body:
THE ORIGINAL WORDING OF THIS CRITERION DEADLOCKED THE CLOSE GATE — recorded in full, because I
changed an acceptance criterion and that should never be silent.

The close gate rejected this ticket with:
  "The tickets closing comment explicitly invokes this criterion and declares CLOSING AS WONT-FIX,
   but the ticket system status remains in_progress ... The criterion requires the ticket to be
   closed, not merely for a comment to assert closure."

The verifier read it correctly. The criterion is UNSATISFIABLE BY CONSTRUCTION:
  - closing requires every AC to pass (gate 433c),
  - this AC passes only once the ticket is closed,
  => a self-referential deadlock no amount of work can break.
Read plainly, the original sentence is not an acceptance criterion at all. It is an INSTRUCTION to the
author about which OUTCOME to choose ("the correct outcome is to CLOSE THIS AS WONT-FIX"). Outcomes are
actions taken, not conditions verified. As a checkbox it can only ever refer to itself.

WHAT I CHANGED, and what I deliberately did NOT change:
  - Reworded the criterion to state its VERIFIABLE content: the measurement is recorded on this ticket and
    the wont-fix decision is documented with its rationale.
  - Kept the ORIGINAL WORDING verbatim inside the criterion, so no reader has to take my summary on trust
    or dig through history to see what it used to say.
  - Did NOT weaken the substance. The evidence bar is unchanged and is met: the recoverable saving is zero
    by MECHANISM (a marked span always ending in per-call-unique bytes is write-only by construction), the
    descriptions "already in the cache" premise is disproven at the first differing system byte, and both
    findings are recorded above with citations.
  - Did NOT use --force-close. That would have buried this defect instead of fixing it.

GENERALISABLE DEFECT, not specific to f81d: gate 433c (block close on unchecked AC boxes) turns any
self-referential AC into an unbreakable deadlock, and the phrasing that causes it — "the correct outcome
is to close this as X" — is natural to write when an author wants to pre-authorise a wont-fix. Filed
separately so the AC-authoring guidance can warn about it.
